paragraphs: Ivan left Alyosha and walked home to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. But oddly, a crushing gloom settled on him, and it grew heavier with every step he took toward the house. Being gloomy was nothing odd. What was odd was that Ivan could not say why. He had been low before. And it was hardly surprising that he felt low now, when he had cut every tie that had brought him here and was about to start afresh, that very day, on a new and unknown future. He would be as lonely as ever. He had great hopes, and great—too great—expectations of life, but he could not have said clearly what his hopes were, or his expectations, or even what he wanted.

And yet, although he did feel some dread of the new and unknown, that was not what was troubling him just then. It was something quite different. “Is it disgust at my father’s house?” he wondered. “Quite possibly. I am so sick of it. Even though this is the last time I will step over its hateful threshold, I still hate it.... No, that’s not it either. Is it saying goodbye to Alyosha, and the talk I had with him? For so many years I’ve kept silent with the whole world and never troubled to speak, and then all at once I babble on like that.” It may well have been the annoyance of a young man, inexperienced and vain—annoyance at not having managed to say what he meant, especially to someone like Alyosha, whose understanding his heart had certainly been counting on. That must have played its part, that annoyance. But that was not it, that was not it either. “I’m sick with gloom and yet I can’t say what I want. Maybe it’s better not to think about it.”

Ivan tried “not to think,” but that did no good either. What made his gloom so maddening was that it seemed to have an accidental cause outside himself—he could feel that. Some person or thing seemed to be standing out there somewhere. It is like an object that sometimes forces itself on your eye. You may be so busy with work or talk that for a long time you do not notice it. Yet it nags at you and almost torments you, until at last you realize what it is and take the offending thing away. Often it is something small and absurd—some article left in the wrong place, a handkerchief on the floor, a book not put back on its shelf, and so on.
At last Ivan reached home, cross and in a vile temper. And suddenly, some fifteen paces from the garden gate, he guessed what had been fretting and worrying him.

The valet Smerdyakov was sitting on a bench by the gate, enjoying the evening air. Ivan took one look at him and knew that Smerdyakov was what had been on his mind, and that this was the man his soul could not stand. It all came to him in a flash and was plain. A little earlier, when Alyosha had been telling him of his meeting with Smerdyakov, Ivan had felt a sudden pang of gloom and loathing, and it had at once stirred up anger in answer. Then, as they talked, Smerdyakov had been forgotten for a while. But he had stayed at the back of Ivan’s mind, and as soon as Ivan left Alyosha and started home, the forgotten feeling began to press forward again. “Can a wretched, contemptible creature like that really bother me so much?” he wondered, with unbearable irritation.

It was true that Ivan had come, lately, to feel a strong dislike for the man, especially in the last few days. He had even noticed a feeling growing in him that was close to hatred for the creature. Perhaps the hatred was all the sharper because Ivan had felt quite differently when he first arrived in the neighborhood. At that time he had taken a keen interest in Smerdyakov and had even thought him very original. He had drawn him out in conversation, though he had always been puzzled by a certain incoherence in his mind, or rather a restlessness, and could not understand what it was that so steadily and stubbornly occupied the brain of “the contemplative.” They discussed philosophical questions. They even discussed how there could have been light on the first day, when the sun, moon, and stars were not created until the fourth, and how that was to be understood. But Ivan soon saw that the sun, moon, and stars might be an interesting topic, yet for Smerdyakov they were quite secondary, and he was after something altogether different. In one way or another he began to reveal a boundless vanity—a wounded vanity, too—and Ivan did not like that. That was where his aversion started. Later there was trouble in the house. Grushenka appeared on the scene, and there were the scandals with his brother Dmitri, and they talked about those as well. But although Smerdyakov always spoke of them with great excitement, there was no finding out what he wanted to come of it all. There was, in fact, something startling in the illogic and incoherence of some of his wishes, which slipped out by accident and were always vaguely put. Smerdyakov was forever asking questions, indirect ones, but plainly thought out in advance. What he was after he never explained. Usually, at the most important moment, he would break off and lapse into silence, or turn to some other subject. But what finally irritated Ivan most, and settled his dislike, was the strange and revolting familiarity that Smerdyakov showed more and more. It was not that he forgot himself and was rude. On the contrary, he always spoke very respectfully. Yet he had plainly begun to think—goodness knows why!—that some sort of understanding existed between himself and Ivan Fyodorovitch. He always spoke in a tone that hinted the two of them had a kind of pact, a secret between them, which had at some time been put into words on both sides, and which only they knew and others around them could not grasp. But for a long time Ivan did not see the real cause of his growing dislike, and only lately had he understood what lay at the bottom of it.

Full of disgust and irritation, he tried to slip in at the gate without a word or a look for Smerdyakov. But Smerdyakov got up from the bench, and by that movement alone Ivan knew at once that the man was particularly anxious to talk to him. Ivan looked at him and stopped. That he did stop, instead of walking by as he had meant to a second earlier, made him furious. With anger and disgust he looked at Smerdyakov’s sickly, eunuch-like face, with the little curls combed forward onto the forehead. The left eye winked and the face grinned, as if to say, “Where are you off to? You won’t get past. You see, we two clever fellows have something to say to each other.”

Ivan shuddered. “Get out of my way, you miserable idiot. What have I got to do with you?” was on the tip of his tongue. But to his deep astonishment he heard himself say, “Is my father still asleep, or is he up?”

He asked it softly and meekly, to his own surprise, and at once, to his surprise again, he sat down on the bench. For a moment he felt almost afraid. He remembered that afterwards. Smerdyakov stood facing him with his hands behind his back, looking at him with confidence and something close to sternness.

“His honor is still asleep,” he said, taking his time. (“You spoke first, not I,” he seemed to say.) “You surprise me, sir,” he added after a pause, lowering his eyes with an affected air, putting his right foot forward, and toying with the toe of his polished boot.

“Why do I surprise you?” Ivan asked, curtly and sullenly, struggling hard to keep control. He suddenly realized, with disgust, that he was burning with curiosity and would not for anything have left without having it satisfied.

“Why don’t you go to Tchermashnya, sir?” Smerdyakov suddenly looked up and smiled in his familiar way. “If you are a clever man, you ought to work out for yourself why I am smiling,” his screwed-up left eye seemed to say.
“Why on earth should I go to Tchermashnya?” Ivan asked in surprise.
Smerdyakov said nothing again.

“Fyodor Pavlovitch himself has begged you so hard to,” he said at last, slowly, as if he gave his answer no weight at all. “I’m putting you off with a lesser reason,” he seemed to hint, “just to say something.”
“Damn you! Say what you want!” Ivan shouted at last, in a rage, switching from meekness to violence.
Smerdyakov brought his right foot back beside his left and drew himself up, but he went on looking at him with the same calm and the same little smile.
“Nothing much, really—just for the sake of conversation.”

Another silence followed. For nearly a minute neither spoke. Ivan knew he ought to get up and show his anger. Smerdyakov stood in front of him, and seemed to be waiting to see whether he would get angry or not. At least that was how it seemed to Ivan. At last he made a move to get up. Smerdyakov seemed to seize on that moment.
“I’m in an awful position, Ivan Fyodorovitch. I don’t know what to do with myself,” he said, firmly and clearly, and sighed on the last word. Ivan Fyodorovitch sat down again.

“They’ve both gone completely mad. They’re no better than small children,” Smerdyakov went on. “I mean your father and your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Any minute now Fyodor Pavlovitch will be up and pestering me, ‘Has she come? Why hasn’t she come?’ And so on, every minute, till midnight and even after midnight. And if Agrafena Alexandrovna doesn’t come (and very likely she doesn’t mean to come at all), then he’ll be on at me again in the morning, ‘Why hasn’t she come? When will she come?’—as if it were my fault. And on the other side it’s no better. As soon as it gets dark, or even earlier, your brother turns up with his gun in his hands: ‘Look out, you rogue, you soup-maker. If you miss her and don’t let me know she’s been here—I’ll kill you before anyone.’ And when the night is over, in the morning, he, too, like Fyodor Pavlovitch, starts worrying me half to death. ‘Why hasn’t she come? Will she come soon?’ And he, too, thinks it’s my fault that his lady hasn’t come. And every day and every hour they get angrier and angrier, so that sometimes I think I’ll kill myself from fright. I can’t rely on them, sir.”
“And why did you get mixed up in it? Why did you start spying for Dmitri Fyodorovitch?” Ivan said irritably.

“How could I help getting mixed up in it? Though truly, if you want the plain truth, I haven’t got mixed up in it at all. I kept quiet from the very start, not daring to answer him. But he picked me out to be his servant. Since then he has had one thing only to say: ‘I’ll kill you, you scoundrel, if you miss her.’ I’m certain, sir, that I’ll have a long fit tomorrow.”
“What do you mean, ‘a long fit’?”

“A long fit, one that goes on for a long time—several hours, or maybe a day or two. Once it lasted three days. I fell from the garret that time. The convulsions stopped and then started again, and for three days I couldn’t come to my senses. Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Herzenstube, the doctor here, and he put ice on my head and tried one other remedy too.... I might have died.”
“But they say you can’t tell in advance, with epilepsy, when a fit is coming. So why do you say you’ll have one tomorrow?” Ivan asked, with a strange, irritable curiosity.
“Exactly so. You can’t tell in advance.”
“And anyway, you fell from the garret that time.”
“I climb up to the garret every day. I could fall from the garret again tomorrow. And if not, I could fall down the cellar steps. I have to go down to the cellar every day, too.”
Ivan gave him a long look.
“I can see you’re talking nonsense, and I don’t quite follow you,” he said softly, but with a kind of menace. “Are you saying you’ll pretend to be ill for three days tomorrow, eh?”
Smerdyakov had gone back to staring at the ground and fiddling with the toe of his right foot. Now he put that foot down, moved the left one forward, and said with a grin:

“If I could play a trick like that—that is, fake a fit, which wouldn’t be hard for a man who’s used to them—I would have every right to use such a means to save myself from death. Because even if Agrafena Alexandrovna comes to see his father while I’m lying ill, his honor can’t blame a sick man for not telling him. He’d be ashamed to.”
